g8-2024-004.lessonTitle: Parallel Lines and the Angles in a Triangle
g8-2024-004.quote: the measure of angle EAB equal to the measure of any angle
g8-2024-004.why: The item gives one angle of a triangle (115 degrees) and one angle of its image after a rotation and a reflection (40 degrees), then asks for a third angle, so the student must first know that a rigid motion carries an angle to an equal angle - the 40 is therefore also an angle of ABC - and then take 180 minus 115 minus 40. 'Angle Plus Two' asks those two questions in that order: what the three angles at A sum to, and whether the measure of angle EAB equals the measure of any angle in triangle ABC. The first reading's Unit 1 Lesson 10, 'Composing Figures', is second best: its 'Triangle Plus Two' gets the angle-preservation half (find two pairs of angles that have the same measure) but nothing in Lesson 10 asks for a missing third angle, so the item cannot be finished there.

g8-2024-023.lessonTitle: Parallel Lines and the Angles in a Triangle
g8-2024-023.quote: What is the sum of the angle measures of triangle ABC
g8-2024-023.why: The item asks for an expression, 180 minus (x + y), for the third angle of a triangle whose other two angles are x and y: no figure, no parallel lines, no numbers. A sweep of every grade 8 activity finds none that asks for a missing angle from two known ones, and the curriculum never writes the sum algebraically, so the closest question asked is this Cool-down, which asks for the angle sum of a general triangle and for the reason. I uphold the second reading's lesson but move its evidence from 'Every Triangle in the World' (the argument) to 'Angle Sum' (where the fact itself is tested). The first reading's Unit 1 Lesson 15, 'Adding the Angles in a Triangle', is second best: it is where the 180-degree sum is discovered by tearing the corners off a triangle, but its own tasks only ask whether three given angles can form a triangle, and its reasoning stays with particular cut-out triangles while the item is about any triangle at all.

g8-2024-042.lessonTitle: Parallel Lines and the Angles in a Triangle
g8-2024-042.quote: the structure of parallel lines cut with a transversal to identify alternate interior angles
g8-2024-042.why: NYSED's own exemplary response does this item in two moves: angle ABC is 180 minus 110 and angle ACB is 180 minus 105, both read off the transversals crossing the parallel pair, leaving 35 degrees for angle BAC by the triangle sum. This activity is where the curriculum puts those two moves on one figure - a triangle with a parallel line cut by transversals, angles carried across the parallels, then the 180-degree closure - and Lesson 16 is named for exactly that combination. The first reading's Unit 1 Lesson 14, 'Alternate Interior Angles', is second best: it supplies the transversal half, and its Cool-down chases seven angles across a parallel pair, but there is no triangle anywhere in Lesson 14, so the item cannot be closed there.

g8-2026-025.quote: is the image of trapezoid ABCD under a rigid transformation
g8-2026-025.why: The item gives a triangle and its image under a rotation about the origin and asks which angle-congruence statement is true (angle B congruent to angle Y); the work is deciding which vertex corresponds to which and knowing that a rigid motion carries an angle to an equal angle. This Cool-down asks exactly that pair of things about a figure and its image: label all the vertices of the image, then label all known side lengths and angle measures on both figures. Neither reading wins. The first reading's Unit 1 Lesson 8, 'Rotation Patterns', is about what 180-degree rotations do to segments and its Cool-down only asks whether an image lines up, never which angle matches which. The second reading's Unit 1 Lesson 10, 'Composing Figures', does ask for pairs of angles of equal measure, but inside a composite figure built from three triangles, where the point is the composition; Lesson 7 is where angle preservation itself is established and tested, on one figure and one image, as the item has it.

g8-2023-035.quote: no fractional representation exists for these numbers
g8-2023-035.why: Every answer choice is a claim about the DECIMAL of the square root of 50 - it repeats, it terminates, or it does neither - and the key is the last of those, so the item turns on decimal behaviour rather than on Lesson 4's 'cannot be written as a fraction'. Lesson 17 is the only place the curriculum looks at what an irrational number's decimal actually does: in this activity long division is unavailable because there are no two integers to divide, so students build the decimal of the square root of 2 by successive approximation, and the lesson's own synthesis and summary state the test the item uses - the expansions never end and never repeat. That statement lives in the lesson synthesis and summary, not in any activity task, so the quote here is the definitional line from the activity itself. The first reading's Unit 7 Lesson 4, 'Rational and Irrational Numbers', is second best: it defines irrational as not expressible as a fraction, which is the framing of the item's distractor C rather than of the key, and it never mentions decimals at all.

g8-2024-037.quote: the tilted square is around 1.5 units or a little less
g8-2024-037.why: The item asks which interval the square root of 2 sits in and which end it is nearer: between 1.0 and 1.5 but closer to 1.5. That is this activity's conclusion in so many words - students find the side length of a square of area 2 and see it is around 1.5 units or a little less. The first reading's Unit 7 Lesson 6, 'Reasoning About Square Roots', is second best: its 'Square Root Values' bounds a root between consecutive WHOLE numbers, which only gets the item as far as 'between 1 and 2' and cannot separate the two surviving choices. Unit 7 Lesson 17's 'Some Numbers Are Not Rational' later sharpens the same value to between 1.4 and 1.5, but Lesson 4 is where the item's own level of precision is first reached.

g8-2024-047.quote: Show that they are rational by writing them in the form
g8-2024-047.why: The list (the square root of 49, 1.3 repeating, seven halves, 1.234 and the square root of 32) has to be sorted rational or irrational with the rationals justified - 'be sure to include how you know a number is rational'. That justification is this activity's whole demand: a mixed list of decimals, roots of perfect squares and fractions, shown to be rational by writing each one in fraction form, with the root values chosen exactly because a root can be rational. The first reading's Unit 7 Lesson 4, 'Rational and Irrational Numbers', is second best: its Cool-down asks students to define each kind in their own words and supply their own examples, whereas the item supplies the numbers and asks for the classification plus the fraction test. The repeating member, 1.3 repeating, is only settled one lesson later, in Lesson 17's 'Some Numbers Are Rational'.

g8-2025-042.quote: not all numbers written using square root or cube root notation are irrational
g8-2025-042.why: The item asks students to classify the square root of 1.44; it is 1.2, and the trap is that a decimal under a radical looks irrational. This activity's values were chosen for precisely that trap - its narrative says so in the quoted words - and it asks students to show such numbers are rational by writing them as fractions, which is the justification the item wants. The first reading's Unit 7 Lesson 4, 'Rational and Irrational Numbers', is second best: it is where rational and irrational are defined, but every root Lesson 4 handles is the square root of 2 and irrational, so nothing there rehearses a root that turns out rational.

g8-2026-005.quote: how they might figure out a value for π using measurements of circles
g8-2026-005.why: The item asks which of 0, pi, the square root of 9 and one third is irrational, so the whole item is whether the student has met pi as an irrational number. A search of Unit 7 finds pi named in exactly one lesson - this one - and in this activity, where students approximate the square root of 2 by successive approximation and discuss getting a value for pi from measurements of circles. The first reading's Unit 7 Lesson 4, 'Rational and Irrational Numbers', is second best: its definition does dispose of 0, the square root of 9 and one third, but Lesson 4's only irrational number is the square root of 2 and pi never appears in it. That the square root of 9 is rational is settled in Unit 7 Lesson 16's 'Rational Numbers as Fractions'.

g8-2025-037.quote: rational approximations of irrational numbers to place both rational and irrational numbers
g8-2025-037.why: The item needs the square root of 4 exactly and the square root of 10 approximately, then asks which of four number lines puts P at the total, about 5. This activity is that same mix - plot the square roots of 3, 16 and 30 on one number line - and its narrative names the skill as using rational approximations of irrational numbers to place both kinds of number. The first reading's Unit 7 Lesson 5, 'Square Roots on the Number Line', is second best: it locates a root by drawing a square and comparing its side, a geometric route the item does not need, and it takes one root at a time. Nothing in the curriculum asks for a sum of two square roots except the Warm-up Math Talk that opens Unit 7 Lesson 11, which asks for the square root of 10 plus the square root of 97 to the nearest half.

g8-2025-007.quote: How high up the utility pole does the support pole reach
g8-2025-007.why: This is a situation, not a bare triangle: 20 feet of string as the slant, 15 feet along the ground, and the question is which EQUATION finds the vertical piece x, so the work is reading which given length is the hypotenuse out of a described scene. This Cool-down is the same situation - an 11.5 m support pole whose base is 4.5 m from a vertical utility pole, how high up does it reach - and the item stops one step earlier, at the equation. The first reading's Unit 7 Lesson 9, 'Finding Unknown Side Lengths', is second best: it is where 'which one is the hypotenuse' is drilled, and that is the distinction the distractors test, but Lesson 9 works entirely on drawn or verbally described bare triangles and never asks a student to extract one from a context.

g8-2026-035.quote: The field is 100 meters long and 80 meters wide
g8-2026-035.why: A store 12 miles north and a gas station 16 miles east of the same home, asking the distance between them: a real-world hypotenuse across a right angle that has to be seen in the map first. This activity is the same move - a 100 m by 80 m field crossed diagonally instead of going round two sides - and it is the first place the theorem is used on a described situation rather than a drawn triangle. The first reading's Unit 7 Lesson 9, 'Finding Unknown Side Lengths', is second best: the arithmetic is identical, but Lesson 9's tasks are bare triangles ('a right triangle has sides of length 3, 4, and x') and the item's real work is turning the map into a right triangle. Unit 7 Lesson 13, 'Finding Distances in the Coordinate Plane', is not it either: the item has no coordinate grid.

g8-2025-047.quote: side lengths of the triangle and c is the longest side
g8-2025-047.why: The student wrote 5 squared plus 4 squared equals 3 squared on a diagram of squares drawn on the three sides of a 3-4-5 right triangle, and the item asks for the error and the correct steps - so it is an audit of whether the theorem was applied with the hypotenuse in the right place, and NYSED's exemplary response says exactly that (the legs are 3 and 4, the hypotenuse is 5, so 9 + 16 = 25). This Cool-down is that audit: decide whether a squared plus b squared equals c squared for given triangles, where c is the longest side, and explain how you know. The squares-on-each-side picture with their areas is Lesson 7's own representation, from 'A Table of Triangles'. The first reading's Unit 7 Lesson 8, 'A Proof of the Pythagorean Theorem', is second best - it is the lesson that addresses NY-8.G.6 and the item is about the relationship rather than a computation - but Lesson 8's proof runs on a different picture, two squares of side a + b cut up two ways, and the student's error is a misplaced hypotenuse rather than a flaw in that argument.
